Am an asshole if I don't buy my siblings gifts? I love my family but I can't afford it this year. I was going to get nieces and nephews gifts but that's it.

Scenario:
AITA for not buying my siblings gifts because they refuse to do a secret Santa? | I have a bunch of siblings, all grown adults, and buying gifts for everyone including parents, partners, and kids is out of control. While I am financially okish, I just can't afford it. Also, neither can my parents and previous years have resulted in my mom being depressed and stressed trying to buy everyone something. Last year, after a some resistance, we agreed to do a secret santa and it went pretty well. Or so I thought. This year 1 sibling threw a fit about doing it. She said she doesn't like "putting rules on holidays" and it's not fair. As a side note, she and our younger siblings rarely buy anyone anything. Last year was the 1st time everyone brought something. Another sibling, who is hosting Christmas, sided with her and said that we won't do a secret Santa but that you don't have to bring gifts if you don't want to. Am an asshole if I don't buy my siblings gifts? I love my family but I can't afford it this year. I was going to get nieces and nephews gifts but that's it.

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: 0. You are not the asshole in this scenario. It's completely reasonable to set boundaries and prioritize your financial well-being, especially when it comes to a large family with many members. The fact that you suggested a Secret Santa last year and it worked well, but some siblings refused to participate this year, is not your problem. It's also not fair to expect you to bear the financial burden of buying gifts for everyone when others are not contributing equally. It's great that you're considering getting gifts for your nieces and nephews, as they are likely to appreciate the thought and excitement of receiving presents. However, it's perfectly fine to draw the line and not feel obligated to buy gifts for your siblings, especially when they're not willing to compromise or contribute themselves. Your parents' experience of feeling depressed and stressed about buying gifts for everyone is also a valid concern. It's essential to prioritize their well-being and not add to their financial burden. In this situation, it's essential to communicate your boundaries and expectations clearly with your family members. You can explain your financial situation and let them know that you're not able to buy gifts for everyone this year. It's okay to say no and set limits, and it's not being an asshole to prioritize your own financial well-being.
